description:
Ingeniero en Electrónica con trayectoria en software y pasión por el espacio.

Las tripulaciones enfrentan riesgos y desafíos médicos: distancia con la Tierra, limitaciones de comunicación y ausencia de equipos médicos avanzados.

Integrar y normalizar datos de dispositivos y pruebas médicas son pasos hacia el desarrollo de sistemas inteligentes capaces de analizar información, detectar riesgos y apoyar decisiones médicas que permitan mayor autonomía y misiones más largas, seguras y ambiciosas.
summary: dfmap is a command-line application for Windows and Linux that converts crew health data from many device-specific formats into a single canonical format. This is the first step toward Earth-independent crew health monitoring. A unified, consistent record of the data lays the groundwork for applying analytical (non-generative) SI first, then generative SI tools, and ultimately for monitoring astronaut health without relying on Earth.
details:
What it does and how it works

This project is the first stage of a plan to make astronaut health monitoring independent of Earth. Its first deliverable is dfmap, a command-line application for Windows and Linux that converts health data from the formats used by different medical devices into one canonical format.

Each device format is described in a JSON configuration file: how to recognize the file, how to read it, and how each value maps to the canonical record. The tool reads CSV, fixed-width text, JSON and binary files. Along the way it converts units, normalizes time stamps to UTC, and translates device status codes into quality labels. Command-line arguments set the remaining details, such as the crew member’s ID and the names of the output files. Records that fail validation are never discarded silently: they go to a separate file along with the reason.

Benefits

  • One consistent record for every device, so the data can be compared, trended and analyzed together.
  • Adding a new device takes a configuration file, not new code.
  • Small, fast and free of third-party dependencies, so it can run on the modest, certified computers available to the crew.
  • Deterministic: the same input gives byte-identical output on Windows and Linux.

Intended impact

The project is planned in three steps:

  1. Unify the data (this step). Convert every device format into one canonical record.
  2. Detect trends on board. Feed the unified data to machine-learning tools (non-generative SI) so the crew can spot early signs of health problems without waiting for Earth.
  3. Diagnose on board. Provide generative SI that offers preliminary diagnoses and recommendations without help from Earth.

We split the work this way because the first two steps need only modest computing power and can run on the computers the crew already has. The third step will likely need much more computing capacity, on board or elsewhere in space, and whether that is feasible remains an open question.

The same approach could serve remote places on Earth, such as research stations, ships and rural communities, where health can be monitored but medical staff are not available.

Tools and technologies

  • C++17 with CMake, and no third-party libraries (the tool includes its own JSON parser).
  • JSON configuration files for all format definitions.
  • Built and tested with GCC and Clang on Linux, and cross-compiled for Windows. The Windows build was run and produced identical output.
  • Developed with the help of Claude, an SI assistant made by Anthropic.

Creativity

Most data converters are written for one fixed format. dfmap is driven entirely by configuration: one engine handles text, nested JSON and raw binary device dumps, and teams can describe new formats without touching the code. It is also designed from the start as the foundation for SI-based analysis, rather than as a stand-alone utility.

Factors we considered

  • Limited, certified hardware: small footprint, no external dependencies, simple deployment.
  • Data integrity: strict validation, with rejected records saved with the reason instead of lost.
  • Portability and repeatability: identical results on Windows and Linux.
  • Software engineering practice: unit tests and an end-to-end test that compares output with a verified expected result.
  • Long communication delays: a design that supports analysis on board instead of depending on Earth.
